extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on examining compliance with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112 (and pre-AIA equivalents), including how species and genus claims may be supported, examiner burdens, reply handling, and common circumstances that raise written-description issues. Focused on making complete patentability determinations and communicating findings in Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description support for a claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of a claimed species may be shown by disclosure of an actual reduction to practice, drawings, a complete description of structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, or a combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and lead one of skill in the art to conclude possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of any combination of identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention is sufficient. In mature predictable arts, a method-of-making and function disclosure may be enough to support product claims; in emerging or unpredictable arts, more evidence is required. Disclosure of only a method of making and the function may be insufficient for a product claim (except product-by-process where the process actually produced the product). Partial structure without additional characterization may be insufficient. Reduction to practice corroborates conception; if acts in the specification cannot be performed or product not shown to be produced, written description may not be satisfied. (Cited authorities: Eli Lilly; Fiers; Amgen; Burroughs Wellcome.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description support for a claimed genus
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported by description of a representative number of species, reduction to drawings, or disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics with a structure-function correlation), or combinations thereof, sufficient to show applicant was in possession of the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'representative number of species' must reflect the variation within the genus; where there is substantial variation, a sufficient variety of species must be described. For unpredictable arts, one species will generally not support a broad genus unless the disclosure indicates that the inventor invented species sufficient to constitute the genus or a reasonable structure-function correlation is established (either in the specification or known in the art). Examples where single-species disclosure was insufficient or sufficient are discussed (AbbVie; Enzo; Noelle; Rasmussen; In re Herschler; In re Smythe). If representative species are not disclosed, the genus claim must be rejected for lack of adequate written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective standard for compliance (possession test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that the inventor had possession of what is now claimed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry asks whether the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed. Possession can be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, actual reduction to practice, or by showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., drawings or structural formulas). (Cited authorities: In re Gosteli; Vas-Cath; Lockwood; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Each claim limitation must be supported
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an explicit limitation is not present in the written description, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at the filing date that the description requires that limitation. Each claim must include all elements the applicant described as essential. If the original disclosure does not provide support for each limitation, or an element described as essential is omitted from the claim, the claim (or priority/benefit claim) must be rejected/denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner initial burden to challenge written description adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must have a reasonable basis and present evidence or reasoning by a preponderance of evidence explaining why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure the invention defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting the lack of written description conclusion. These findings should (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention in view of the disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. When appropriate, examiners should suggest claim amendments that can be supported by the application, mindful of the prohibition on introducing new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action completeness and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) and clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and their bases in any Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review proposed rejections and their bases to confirm correctness before imposing a rejection. The Office action should clearly explain findings and reasons and, when possible, offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling applicant reply and reexamination of written description rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon reply by applicant, the examiner must reperform the written description analysis in view of the whole record, including amendments, arguments, and evidence submitted by applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record shows the written description requirement is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If the record still does not demonstrate adequacy, the examiner may repeat the rejection but must fully respond to applicant's rebuttal arguments and properly treat any further showings submitted in the reply. Affidavits relevant to written description must be thoroughly analyzed and discussed in the next Office action. (Cited authority: In re Alton.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments/new claims must be supported in original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing an amendment, an applicant should show support in the original disclosure for new or amended claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should specifically point out the support for any amendments to disclosure. Examiners should not reject on 'new matter' grounds when the issue is one of written description (but should follow MPEP §2163.06 for new matter objections). If claim language departs from the disclosure of the application as filed, the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application, resulting in rejection or denial of benefit/priority as appropriate. (See MPEP §§714.02 and 2163.06.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations that typically raise written description issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description issues commonly arise in: amendments affecting a claim; reliance on the filing date of a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120; reliance on foreign priority or provisional filing dates under 35 U.S.C. 119; claims corresponding to a count in an interference; original claims that may be insufficiently described; and indefiniteness re means/step-plus-function limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each circumstance has particular considerations (e.g., an amendment to claims must be supported by the original description; claims relying on earlier filing dates must be disclosed in earlier applications in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a)). Examples and cases are cited for each typical circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claim may lack written description (functional and broad genus claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: An original claim may lack written description support when it defines the invention in functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed, or when a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure only describes a narrow species with no evidence the genus was contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere appearance of words in the specification or claim does not necessarily satisfy the requirement; the specification must describe the claimed invention so that one skilled in the art can recognize what is claimed. (Cited authorities: Ariad v. Eli Lilly; Enzo Biochem v. Gen-Probe.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter need not be described in haec verba, but departures indicate lack
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the claim need not be literally described using the same terms in order to satisfy the written description requirement, but if a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed—i.e., involving a departure from, addition to, or deletion from the disclosure—the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conclusion results in rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112, first paragraph) or denial of the benefit of a prior filing/priority date, as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency and inherent disclosure standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the doctrine of inherent disclosure, when a specification describes an invention that has certain undisclosed yet inherent properties, that specification can serve as adequate written description to support a later application that explicitly recites those inherent properties, but inherency must be more than probabilities or possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence to establish inherency must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and that persons of ordinary skill would recognize it. The mere fact something may result from given circumstances is not sufficient. (Cited authorities: In re Robertson; Kennecott; Yeda Research.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Means- (or step-) plus-function limitations and corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation expressed in means- or step-plus-function language shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof. If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the entire claimed function, the limitation is indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such indefiniteness arises because the applicant has failed to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA 112, second paragraph). Examiners should assess whether sufficient corresponding structure/acts are present in the specification to support the claimed function.
